title: Arrays: the everyday methods
goal: Add, remove, find and copy array items confidently, knowing which methods change the original array.

concepts: Creating arrays, length, indexing, at(-1)
Mutating methods: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse
Non-mutating methods: slice, concat, includes, indexOf, join, toSorted
Copying arrays with [...arr] and why = doesn't copy
Array.isArray and Array.from
Arrays hold references: two variables can point to the same array

build.task: In day31/, write playlist.js: manage a playlist array of song titles with functions addSong(list, song) (no duplicates), removeSong(list, song), moveSong(list, from, to), shuffle(list) (returns a NEW shuffled array, original unchanged; use Fisher–Yates), and nowPlaying(list, index) that wraps around at the end. Decide for each whether it mutates or returns a new array, and write that in a comment above it. Add at least 12 checks, including one proving shuffle doesn't change the original.
acceptance: Each function has a comment saying 'mutates' or 'returns new array'
addSong refuses duplicates (case-insensitive is a bonus)
moveSong uses splice correctly for moves forward and backward
shuffle returns a new array and the original is unchanged (checked)
nowPlaying(list, list.length) returns the first song
At least 12 passing checks

hints: Moving an item: const [item] = list.splice(from, 1); list.splice(to, 0, item);
Fisher–Yates: copy the array, then loop i from the end down to 1, pick j = random 0..i, and swap a[i] and a[j].
To compare arrays in checks, compare JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b). === on two arrays compares references, not contents.

explainBack.q: Which of your functions mutate the array and which return a new one? Why did you choose that for shuffle?
lookFor: shuffle returns new so original order is kept
mutation can surprise other code holding the same array

explainBack.q: Why does const b = a not copy an array? What does?
lookFor: both variables reference the same array
change through one shows in the other
[...a] or a.slice() makes a shallow copy

lastHintExplanation: Arrays are objects, and a variable holds a reference to them. const b = a makes b point to the same array, so mutating either one changes both. [...a] or a.slice() makes a new (shallow) copy. Returning a new array from shuffle leaves the caller's data untouched, which avoids surprise bugs.

predict.q: const a = [1, 2, 3]; const b = a; b.push(4); console.log(a.length)
predict.why: a and b point to the same array; const prevents reassignment, not mutation.

dsa.note: Use a Set or Map to avoid nested loops.

  { title: 'Inception', year: 2010, rating: 8.8, minutes: 148, genre: 'Sci-Fi', language: 'English' },

acceptance: No for/while loops in the answer functions
All 8 questions answered by separate, well-named functions
reduce always has an initial value
Sorting doesn't change the original movies array (copy first or use toSorted)
Each answer has a passing check; average rating is rounded to 2 decimals

hints: Load the data with const { movies } = require('./movies.js'); at the top of your answers file.
Count per genre: movies.reduce((acc, m) => { acc[m.genre] = (acc[m.genre] ?? 0) + 1; return acc; }, {}).
Longest movie: reduce comparing minutes, starting with movies[0]. Top 3: [...movies].sort((a, b) => b.rating - a.rating).slice(0, 3).

explainBack.q: Walk through your genre-count reduce step by step for the first two movies.
Why must the sort compare function return a - b (or b - a)? What happens without it?

lastHintExplanation: reduce walks the array carrying an accumulator: it starts with the initial value you give (here {}), and each callback returns the updated accumulator for the next item. Without an initial value, the first element becomes the accumulator, which breaks object-building and crashes on empty arrays. sort's compare function returns negative to put a first, positive to put b first; without it, items are compared as strings.

predict.why: With braces, an arrow function needs an explicit return.
reduce on an empty array with no initial value throws a TypeError.

title: Objects: properties, methods, destructuring and spread
goal: Model real things as objects and copy, merge and read them safely with modern syntax.

concepts: Object literals, dot vs bracket notation, dynamic keys
Methods and this (inside regular functions vs arrow functions)
Object.keys, Object.values, Object.entries, and for...of over entries
Destructuring objects and arrays, with defaults and renaming
Spread {...obj} for copying/merging and rest for collecting
Optional chaining ?. for safe deep reads
Shallow vs deep copy; structuredClone

build.task: In day33/, build a tiny student-records module. Create createStudent({ name, rollNo, marks = {}, address }) returning an object with methods average(), best() (subject with highest mark), and summary(). Write updateMarks(student, subject, mark) that returns a NEW student object (original unchanged), mergeSettings(defaults, userSettings) using spread, and getCity(student) using optional chaining that returns 'Unknown' if there's no address. Show the shallow-copy trap: copy a student with spread, change a mark in the copy, and log that the original changed too; then fix it with structuredClone.
acceptance: createStudent uses parameter destructuring with a default
Methods use this correctly (regular function syntax for methods)
updateMarks returns a new object; a check proves the original is unchanged
getCity works for students with and without an address (no crash)
Shallow-copy trap demonstrated and fixed with structuredClone, with comments
At least 10 passing checks

hints: Methods: average() { const vals = Object.values(this.marks); ... }. Arrow functions don't get their own this, so they don't work as methods here.
updateMarks: return { ...student, marks: { ...student.marks, [subject]: mark } }. The inner spread matters.

explainBack.q: Why did updateMarks need a nested spread for marks? What breaks without it?
Why didn't you use arrow functions for the methods?
lookFor: arrow functions don't have their own this
this would be the outer scope, not the object
stops and returns undefined if address is null/undefined

lastHintExplanation: Spread makes a shallow copy: the top-level properties are copied, but nested objects like marks are still shared references, so you must spread them too. Regular-function methods get this from the object they're called on; arrow functions take this from the surrounding scope, so they don't work as object methods. ?. returns undefined instead of throwing when the left side is null or undefined.

predict.q: const a = { x: { y: 1 } }; const b = { ...a }; b.x.y = 2; console.log(a.x.y)
predict.why: Spread is shallow: a.x and b.x are the same object.

predict.q: const { name: n = 'Anon' } = { name: undefined }; console.log(n)
predict.why: The default applies when the value is undefined; the variable is renamed to n.

explainBack.q: Explain each cleaning step and which rows it fixed.
What's the difference between a JavaScript object and JSON text?
lookFor: parse turns text into objects; stringify the reverse

lastHintExplanation: JSON is text: a string format with double-quoted keys and no functions, undefined or comments. Real data is messy, so validate every field: strip commas before Number(), reject non-finite results, and normalise text before grouping, or 'pune' and 'PUNE' become separate cities.

build.task: In day35/, write text-tools.js with: slugify('Hello World! 2025') → 'hello-world-2025'; titleCase; countWords; maskPhone('9876543210') → '******3210'; isValidPincode (6 digits, not starting with 0) using a regex; and initials('asha rani verma') → 'ARV'. hints: slugify: lowercase, replace anything that isn't a-z or 0-9 with '-', then collapse repeated dashes and trim dashes from the ends: .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, '').
Pincode regex: /^[1-9][0-9]{5}$/. ^ and $ make it match the whole string.

explainBack.q: Explain your pincode regex character by character.
How does your ageFromDob handle a birthday later this year?
lookFor: then subtract 1 if this year's birthday hasn't come

lastHintExplanation: In /^[1-9][0-9]{5}$/, ^ and $ anchor the whole string, [1-9] is a first digit that isn't zero, and [0-9]{5} is exactly five more digits. For age, subtract the birth year from this year, then subtract one more if this year's birthday hasn't happened yet (compare month, then day). JavaScript months are 0-based.

predict.q: const d = new Date(2026, 0, 31); d.setDate(d.getDate() + 1); console.log(d.getMonth(), d.getDate())
predict.why: Jan 31 + 1 day rolls over to Feb 1: month 1 (0-based), day 1.
Strings are immutable; the assignment is silently ignored.

hints: Log delivered right after the filter. Is it empty? Look at the braces in the arrow function.
Once delivered has items, revenue looks strange. What does reduce use as sum on the first call when no initial value is given?

explainBack.q: List the 5 bugs and the one-line fix for each.

sort without compare function / wrong direction

lastHintExplanation: 1) An arrow function with braces needs return, so the filter kept nothing. 2) reduce without an initial value uses the first order object as sum; pass 0. 3) .sort() compares strings and ascends; use (a, b) => b - a. 4) perCustomer[name] starts undefined, and undefined + n is NaN; use (perCustomer[name] ?? 0) + n. 5) map that assigns o.amount mutates the originals; return { ...o, amount: ... } instead.
